messages.subject: Suppress INLA-SPDE notes?
messages.body_plain:
We've written a function that uses INLA-SPDE in the background to do part of our analysis. When calling INLA (in fact only the first time a user does that in a given session), a NOTE is printed saying:

Note: method with signature ‘TsparseMatrix#Matrix#missing#replValue’ chosen for function ‘[<-’,
 target signature ‘dgTMatrix#ngCMatrix#missing#numeric’.
 "Matrix#nsparseMatrix#missing#replValue" would also be valid

I understand this is not a problem --- in fact it doesn't happen when you re-run our function in the same session. But, as our function is intended for users who are probably not familiar with the whole INLA-SPDE machinery, we'd like to avoid printing this message. Is this possible at all?

Thanks
Gianluca

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Suppress INLA-SPDE notes?
messages.body_plain:
I found the code I was thinking of,
  options(list("Matrix.quiet"=TRUE))
but that doesn't actually turn off these messages.  Looking in the
change log for the Matrix package indicates that that instead relates
to other types of messages, such as in the qr decomposition method,
see
   ?"sparseQR-class"

The problem with the "Note:" messages is that they are generated by
the S4 object system in the R language, and therefore hard to pin down
individually.
Since they are not warnings, don't use suppressWarnings(), as that
would disable _actual_ warnings!
A safer option is to use suppressMessages():

In new R session:
  library(INLA)
  Q=inla.spde.precision(inla.spde2.matern(inla.mesh.create(globe=4)),theta=c(0,0))
This should produce the Note:s.

In another new R session:
  library(INLA)
  suppressMessages({Q=inla.spde.precision(inla.spde2.matern(inla.mesh.create(globe=4)),theta=c(0,0))})
This should _not_ produce the Note:s.  Other types of potentially
informative notes will also be disabled however,
so it's not a perfect solution.

Finn

Unfortunately these messages can happen in any place that does any sparse matrix operation, and the precise trigger depends on user input, so covering all possibilities in that way would be difficult; I've had messages appearing far into a long and complex R session.
We'd have to add a "dummy calculation" for every encountered case, and it's not necessarily clear how to construct a case that would trigger a specific Note.  That said, it shouldn't hurt to add dummy calculations that we _do_ know would trigger a Note.

Finn

Just a minor comment to this issue.

If you want to define some of the nodes in a modelcomponent to some
fixed values, an easier trick (which will give the correct normalization
constant), is to define this as

	Ax = e

and define this in 'extraconstr'. This will add one 'solve' for each
constr. However, since defining x[1] = 1, f.ex, will make that model
component singular, you need to add some noise, like

	f(..., diagonal = 1e-8)

which will ensure that x[1] = 1, say, almost (like observed with a high
variance).

ensuring that x[1] = 1, say, using an additional likelihood, would be a
little more cumbersome, will not adjust the normalising constant of that
model component, BUT, but be computationally cheaper.

messages.subject: survival data and SPDE model
messages.body_plain:
Hello to all INLA experts,

I am wondering if an SPDE-type latent spatial field could be used with survival data in RINLA.
>From what I understand, inla.stack does not accept data of class inla.surv, so this cannot be implemented straightforwardly (?).  I am not sure if there is a conceptual problem with such an approach or if it is just not implemented? Could there be a simple workaround for the current implementation (without using inla.surv or inla.stack)?

This kind of spatial approach may not be useful for typical survival data, but I have in mind to "abuse" the survival framework for the modeling of spatial extremes, e.g. of wind speeds, where the left-censored Weibull would be an appropriate univariate distribution for threshold exceedances.

My basic code is given below.

Thank you for any help,

Best

Thomas

#coord and data or given coordinate and data matrices
#the latent model should be of the AR(1)-SPDE type, similar to the Cameletti et al. paper

mesh <- inla.mesh.2d(loc=coord, offset=-.1, max.edge=50)
spde <- inla.spde2.matern(mesh=mesh, alpha=2)

#data is matrix with days (rows) and observation sites (30 columns)
n.group <- nrow(data)
#transform into format with columns for site, day, obs
data <- cbind(rep(1:ncol(data), each=nrow(data)), rep(1:nrow(data), ncol(data)), as.numeric(data))
colnames(data) <- c("site", "day", "obs")

#use threshold exceedances
thr <- quantile(data[,3], .9)
event <- rep(1, nrow(data))
event[data[,3] < thr] <- 2
data.surv <- inla.surv(time=data.sel[,3], event=event)

field.indices <- inla.spde.make.index("field", n.spde=spde$n.spde, n.group=n.group)
A.est <- inla.spde.make.A(mesh, loc=coord[data[,1],], group=data[,2], n.group=n.group)

#here I would like to make an appropriate call to inla.stack using data.surv for the data argument
#however, this seems not to be possible

stack.est <- inla.stack(...)

A <- inla.stack.A(stack.est)
form <- (resp ~ -1 + Intercept + f(field, model=spde, group=field.group, control.group = list(model="ar1")))
fit <- inla(form, family="weibull", data=inla.stack.data(stack.est, spde=spde),
            control.predictor=list(A=inla.stack.A(stack.est), compute=TRUE),
            control.compute=list(cpo=FALSE),
            control.inla = list(reordering = "metis"),
            keep=FALSE, verbose=TRUE)

Hi,

I've attached code for running Dirichlet boundary models.
The syntax for the helper functions is basically the same as for the
regular functions,
but it supports just a small subset of the features.
The code runs both Neumann and Dirichlet models, so you can see the differences.

I believe the latest excursions package contains features helping with
extracting the relevant
parts of the predictor, this works in exactly the same way for Neumann
and Dirichlet
models, since the predictions are not tied to the internal size of the
model itself.
It's only when looking at summary.random$field that the user will
notice any difference.

The example also compares what happens for simple model
misspecification; running a
Neumann model on Dirichlet data, and a Dirichlet model on Neumann data.
At least for the simple boundary in the example, it's safer to use a Neumann
model, but it may be different for more complicated models.

Note that the example includes an intercept, so that the complete model can have
an arbitrary value on the boundary.  For true Neumann, just don't
include the intercept.

The example does not support soap film smoothing, since that would
involve a model
for the boundary values as well.  This is also doable, but messier, as
it will involve more
parameters.  Future inla version may include that.

Finn

> models, since the predictions are not tied to the internal size of the
> model itself.

> notice any difference.
>
> The example also compares what happens for simple model
> misspecification; running a
> Neumann model on Dirichlet data, and a Dirichlet model on Neumann data.
> At least for the simple boundary in the example, it's safer to use a Neumann
> model, but it may be different for more complicated models.
>
> Note that the example includes an intercept, so that the complete model can have
> an arbitrary value on the boundary.  For true Neumann, just don't
> include the intercept.
>
> The example does not support soap film smoothing, since that would

On 4 May 2015, at 23:00, Eric Coker <esc...@gmail.com> wrote:

> My hunch is that its not a memory issue (though it may well be) since I have 12GB memory available and I'm only using 20 stations that consists of daily 7077 measurements total.

It's not the number of observations that limits it, it's the size of the model; in your case the size of the mesh times the number of timepoints.

As for "missing" observations, a short rant: if you have 500 mesh nodes, say, and only 20 observation locations, then at least 480 potential observations are "missing", so whether all 20 locations were observed or only 18, say, is fairly irrelevant, and when thinking of the continuous interpretation of the model, infinitely many observations are missing! The whole concept of missingness isn't really applicable to these types of problems.  (Though it is entirely reasonable in other contexts, in particular for estimation algorithms depending on specific data coverage structures.)
The simplest way to "specify" missingness is the obvious one: only supply data that was actually observed.  The second simplest one is to supply covariates but an NA "observation", which simply means that you'll get a prediction for an unobserved location, as it produces the posterior distribution at that potential observation location.  Not surprisingly, this is also the method used
to obtain spatial predictions in general.
The important issue is rather if the data that _was_ observed is informative about the model parameters or not.

Finn

messages.subject: Spatial misalignment
messages.body_plain:
Dear All,

We try to estimate the relationship between a health outcome (Y = total deaths) at the municipal level and an exposure variable X ( soil pollution ) observed at point level in the whole country.
The model we consider is the following:

X_j ~  Gamma( mu_j )

Y_i ~ Poisson (E_i R_i)

where E_i is the expected number of cases and

(1) log( mu_j ) = alpha_X + x( s_j )

(2) log( R_i ) = alpha_Y + beta*x( s_i ) +  U_i

where
- alpha_X and alpha_Y are some constant parameters
- x( s ) is the realization of a Gaussian Field at location s.
- The locations s_j correspond to the observation points of soil pollution
- The locations s_i correspond to the municipality centroids.
- U_i is an additional spatial effect ( U_i ~ BYM ).

The results provided by INLA are fairly consistent.
But, we have two major concerns about this model:
1.  In INLA, the linear predictor must be gaussian. However, is there a way to model in equation (2) a "not so linear" relationship with the latent variable x(s) like a spline or a factor (e.g., ns(x(s),3) or factor(x(s),4))?
2. We use the SPDE approach to approximate the Gaussian Field x(s) on a mesh created using the inla.mesh.2d() function at location points of soil pollution observations. On the other hand, the additional spatial effect U_i in equation (2) is a BYM based on a neighbourhood structure of the municipalities. Is there a way to model on the same support both spatial effects (x(s) and U).
Thanks in advance for your help.

support formulation unless you use a data augmentation scheme (see the

average of an SPDE model over the region. This can be done with
inla.spde.make.block.A.  But be careful: THIS IS NOT THE SAME AS THE
BYM.

I want to forecast disease risk using the INLA package. Let me introduce my data first. I have read some references written by  Ramiro Ruiz-Cardenas (e.g., Fitting dynamic models using integrated nested Laplace approximations - INLA), but no example is related to forecast. Dose anyone could help me out? thank you so much!

Regards

Yi

outcome observed for 1995).

ahead. Our experience is that random effects (like dynamic intercepts)
are not good to forecast as to fit the data. In the example above you

In the example we have the model
   y_t ~ Poisson(\lambda_t)
   \lambda_t = E_t R_t = E(y_t)

at risk in 2010 to compute E_t+1. However, R_t+1 can be predicted
considering E_t+1=1
